newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - A speculative rally lifts zinc.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - A speculative rally lifts zinc.

text.p: The price of zinc extended a speculative rally to end Wednesday at $1,463 per tonne, its highest in almost seven years on the London Metal Exchange.
Only two weeks ago zinc was trading around $1,350 before concerns about tight prompt supply took hold.
"It (the advance) is due to the weight of money that is going into it at the moment," Robin Bhar, analyst at LME trader Brandeis said.

Talk continued to circulate that some metal being delivered from China into Singapore is old and of doubtful quality, although China's Zhuzhou smelter said on Monday that Swiss trader Glencore, which had been querying the quality of its 'TORCH' brand of zinc, had withdrawn a complaint made to the LME.
Traders said the talk of complaints reflects a battle between major longs and shorts. In the latter case some say there is a large Chinese investment position now some $300 under the market.
"They have been selling zinc for ages - the question is whether they are going to deliver against these shorts," one noted.

Gold extended its latest slide when it slipped to its lowest fixing since March 24, 1993 during London's Wednesday morning, although it managed to edge slightly up from the lows by the afternoon setting.
Fears of central bank selling, lack of investor interest and sales by producers who are seeking to protect profits against even lower prices have flattened the gold market this week.
Gold was fixed at $332.15 per ounce at 1400 GMT, up from $331.45 in the morning but still under Tuesday's $333.70.

One analyst said a developing El Nino warm ocean current might have an impact on the gold market if, as has happened before, it results in a poor Indian monsoon. Bad rains may hit harvests, crimp farm incomes and reduce demand for gold in rural India.

"There are signs of a major El Nino effect which could bring India its first poor monsoon in seven years," the analyst said. "The strength of the agricultural sector has driven the boom in demand for gold in India."

World coffee prices were again firm after rallying on Tuesday as a strike hit Brazil's big Santos port and cold weather approached that country's coffee belt and revived fears in the market of a possible frost.
Benchmark September robusta coffee futures hit a high of $1860 a tonne in London on Tuesday, then eased, only to recover to end Wednesday at $1840.

On the grain markets, soybeans fell further in Chicago in a bruising selloff that began on Monday. The sell-off was triggered by a U.S. Department of Agriculture report that put 1997 U.S. soybean acreage well above consensus expectations.
Some key prices at 1745 GMT.
